figures.caption: FIG. 1. Self-Organized Feedforward Connectivity. A, Schematic of the two-layer model after learning. An input layer of neurons R(x, t), encoding a unidirectionally moving stimulus at speed v through Gaussian tuning curves, projects through a Gaussian connectivity profile to a second layer U(x, t) that implements competition via Hebbian learning, firing-rate adaptation, and global inhibition (see Eqs. 2, 3 and 6). B, Learned standard deviation as a function of the β parameter. Red: simulation median and interquartile ranges; black dashed line: theoretical prediction (Eq. 13). Simulations were performed using the Euler method with a time step of ∆t = 5 · 10−3 s. Parameters used: Nin = Nc = 512, k = 5.12 · 10−2 cm4s2/syn, τ = 15 ms, τv = 600 ms, σR = 5 cm, ηJ = 5 · 10−4 Hz, m = 0.2, AR = 30 Hz, αJ = 1, v = 26.8 cm/s. C, As B, but for learned weight amplitude, using the same parameters. Simulation results are summarized by the median and interquartile ranges across neurons, with the dashed line indicating the theoretical prediction (Eq. 12). D, Evolution of the feedforward connectivity matrix over time. Random initial weights gradually converge to a smooth Gaussian profile, enabling the competitive layer to develop a continuous spatial code.

FIG. 2. Global stability analysis across inhibition factor and coupling strength. Numerical spectral analysis of the generalized eigenvalue problem shows the dependence of the real part of the leading eigenvalue, λmax, on the input density ρin and synaptic damping strength αJ , for different values of β. The system is stable whenever ℜ(λi) < 0 for all modes; accordingly, the curves report − ln(−λmax). Across the explored parameter range, λmax remains negative, indicating robust stability. Panels correspond to the specified β values. Colors indicate αJ from 0.001 to 100. Spectral analysis was performed with a spatial resolution of ∆s = 0.1 cm and system parameters L = 100 cm, m = 0.15, τ = 15 ms, τv = 600 ms, k = 0.01 cm4s2/syn, ηJ = 5 · 10−4 Hz, AR = 30 Hz, σR = 5 cm, and ρin = Nin/L, with Nin ranging from 512 to 5000 neurons (across the tested parameter range, no eigenvalues with positive real parts were observed).

FIG. 3. Dependence of bump asymmetry γ on adaptation strength and input speed. A, Level curves of constant γ in the (m, τv√ 2σ ) parameter space, showing how combinations of adaptation strength m and input velocity v give rise to different bump asymmetries. B, Theoretical predictions (dashed black lines) and simulation results (red stars) for γ as a function of m, for three fixed values of input velocity v. Each curve corresponds to a different v, illustrating the modulation of bump asymmetry by the speed of external input as well as its monotonic dependence on m. Simulations were performed using the Euler method with a time step of ∆t = 5 · 10−3 s. Parameters used: Nin = Nc = 1000, k = 0.1 cm4s2/syn, τ = 10 ms, τv = 800 ms, σR = 5 cm, AR = 30 Hz.

FIG. 4. Self-organized multilayer architecture potentiates predictive coding. A, Schematic of the multilayer model after learning. Each layer successfully learns to encode space. Additionally, each layer encodes a position that is shifted into the future relative to its preceding input layer. B, The learning process for each of the four layers. The plot shows the correlation between each layer’s feedforward connectivity matrix and the theoretically expected Gaussian profile. Despite being initialized with random weights, all layers converge to a high correlation, indicating that they all learn to encode space. C, An example of the activity bump in each layer compared to the original input signal. The spatial shift, or prediction into the future, increases progressively with the layer number. D, The predictive shift as a function of the layer number. The model’s theoretical prediction ∆i = Liγσu, with Li the number of layer (dashed black line). Stars denote the median shift computed over 100 positions uniformly sampled in [0, L), with error bars indicating the corresponding interquartile range. All shown results correspond to simulations performed using the Euler method with a time step of ∆t = 5 · 10−3 s and done for the set of parameters τ = 15 ms, τv = 600 ms, m = 0.25, σR = 5 cm, AR = 30 Hz, ηJ = 5 · 10−4 Hz, αJ = 0.5, k = 0.01 cm4s2/syn, L = 70 cm, and v = 20 cm/s, Nin = Nc = 512 for all layers (including input).

FIG. 5. Recurrent attractor connectivity can be learned from an input tutor. A, Schematic of the two layer network after learning both feedforward and recurrent connectivity. B, The learning process for both recurrent and feedforward connectivities. The plot shows the correlation between each connectivity matrix and the theoretically expected Gaussian profile. C, The learned recurrent connectivities allow the network to self-sustain a moving Gaussian bump in the absence of input tutor. The speed of the Gaussian bump satisfies the theoretical prediction Eq. 25. Stars denote the median speed computed over 104 simulation steps (Euler integration, ∆t = 5·10−3 s), with error bars indicating the corresponding interquartile range. Parameters used: Nin = Nc = 512, L = 100 cm, k = 5.12 · 10−1 cm4s2/syn, τ = 15 ms, τv = 600 ms, σR = 5 cm, ηJ = ηW = 5 · 10−4 Hz, AR = 30 Hz, αJ = 1, αW = 8, β = 0.5 and v computed from Eq.25.

FIG. 6. Stability landscape of recurrent connectivity in the (αJ , αW ) parameter space. This figure summarizes how hyperparameter tuning shapes the emergence of recurrent attractor structure in the network. A, Regions of the parameter space in which the learned feedforward (FF) and recurrent (REC) connectivities achieve high correlation with their target Gaussian profiles. Red dots indicate parameter combinations for which neither feedforward nor recurrent connectivity attains a high final correlation. Blue dots indicate cases in which the feedforward connectivity converges to a high-correlation solution, whereas the recurrent connectivity does not. Green dots indicate parameter combinations in which both feedforward and recurrent connectivities converge to high-correlation Gaussian profiles, enabling the system to self-sustain a moving bump of activity. The blue shaded region schematizes the parameter regime in which learned feedforward connectivity is expected, whereas the green shaded region schematizes the regime in which fully stable attractor dynamics are expected. B, Representative examples of the final feedforward connectivity matrices for the parameter combinations indicated in Panel A. C, Representative examples of the final recurrent connectivity matrices for the parameter combinations indicated in Panel A. In both panels B and C, numbers above each matrix correspond to the associated point in the phase diagram. Simulations were performed using the Euler method with a time step of ∆t = 5 · 10−3 s. Simulation parameters: Nin = Nc = 512, τ = 15 ms, τv = 600 ms, m = 0.2, σR = 5 cm, AR = 30 Hz, ηJ = ηW = 10−3 Hz, k = 5.12 · 10−1 cm4s2/syn, L = 100 cm, β = 0.5 and v = 26.8 cm/s.

FIG. 7. Validation of the baseline shift properties. (A) Empirically measured baseline shifts in the U(x, t) and V (x, t) variables, demonstrating adherence to the conservation property. (B) Measured baseline shifts showing consistency with the predicted proportionality property. A consistent colorcoding scheme is maintained across both panels. Simulations were performed using the Euler method with a time step of ∆t = 5 · 10−3 s. Parameters used for simulations: Nc = 1000, L = 100 cm, AW = 1 syn, τ = 10 ms, τv = 100 ms, m = 0.106, k = 1.25 · 10−3 cm4s2/syn, g = 1 cm−3, v0 = 12.59 cm/s.

FIG. 8. Unidirectional path integration under constant and time-varying speed A, The right axis shows the measured standard deviation of the activity profile, std[U(Ispeed)]x, as a function of Ispeed, normalized by its value at Ispeed = 0. The left axis shows the measured baseline shift, ϵuIspeed, normalized by the maximum value of the U(x, t) bump (Umax) for each different Ispeed, theoretically equivalent to Au√ 2πσu . Both quantities exhibit close agreement with the dependence on Ispeed, consistent with Eq. 35. The dashed lines are shown in a red scale and the dots in a blue scale to indicate different m values. B, Measured bump velocities across varying adaptation levels compared against our theoretical prediction (Eq. 36) as a function of the input current Ispeed. The red color scale corresponds to the same set of m values shown in panel A. C, Path integration performance under time-varying speed. The input current modulates the bump velocity in real time. Results were taken from the same simulations used in Fig. 7.

FIG. 9. Velocity formula comparison. (A) Measured versus theoretical speeds are compared across different combinations of time constants (τ and τv, in seconds) indicated in the legend. Both speeds are normalized by their respective σu/τ factors. Each data point represents a distinct m value ranging from 1.01 · τ/τv to 0.25. The green dashed line indicates the identity line, highlighting the discrepancy between theoretical and measured values. The black dashed line represents the linear fit, which yields a slope of 0.7166± 0.0027 (slope ± SE). Other simulation parameters: N = 1000, L = 100 cm, σW = 5 cm, k = 1 cm4s2/syn, and AW = 1 syn. (B) Speed as a function of adaptation strength. Red stars denote simulation results obtained with the same parameters as panel A and specific time constants τ = 15ms and τv = 600ms. The blue dashed curve shows the theoretical prediction from the projection method, while the black dashed curve corresponds to the empirically corrected expression, obtained by rescaling Eq. A28 by a the estimated slope from the linear fit.
